Hi Frank, are you working through your lunch hour again?
No, not at all. It's my tenth wedding anniversary next week, and I promised Jane that
I would book a city break for us as I have annual leave to take, and it would be nice
to celebrate somewhere warm, so I'm trying to book something in Barcelona.
That sounds so romantic. I adore Barcelona. It's such a fabulous cosmopolitan city. There's
so much to do there, excellent food, and that cathedral that they are still building after
about 150 years. Very cool. I know, but the anniversary is looming, and I'm still scrambling
to find accommodation. Everything is either wildly expensive or already fully booked. I'm starting
to feel a bit frantic. Well, if you were going for a whole week, why don't you do a couple of
nights and somewhere really glamorous, and then do the rest of the week a bit further up the coast,
where the accommodation is cheaper, and that will offset the cost of the expensive place?
That might be a good plan. It's not too expensive to rent a car, so we could still drive into the city.
Yes, there are lots of places outside the city that have pools and are all inclusive,
so we wouldn't even need to pay for food or drinks. I'll send a query now about the dates we're
interested in. That sounds perfect. I'm sure that Jane will be absolutely thrilled to bits.
I really do recommend visiting that cathedral. You can go all the way up to the top of it,
but you need to go up a really steep spiral staircase to get there. Considering Jane is terrified
of heights, I think if I tried to make her do that, I would come back divorced. Thanks for the help,
though. It was turning into a logistical nightmare. Questions went to four are based on the conversation
you have just heard. Question 1. What is the man planning to do? Question 2. Why is the man starting
to feel a bit frantic? Question 3. What does the woman suggest the man do? Question 4. What does the
man say about his wife, Jane? Conversation 2. Hey there, Paul. How's it going? Hi, Susan. Just keeping
busy with the usual stuff, filling prescriptions, talking to patients about their medications,
that kind of thing. How about you? Same here. Although I did have an interesting case come in
this morning, a patient came in inquiring about a medication that had a potential interaction with
another medication she was already taking. Oh, that's always tricky. What did you do? I explained
the issue to her as best I could, and recommended she double-check with her doctor. And you know
what? She actually followed my advice, and the doctor ended up switching the patient's medication.
That's great. You must feel quite accomplished. Totally. These moments are the highlights of my
routine work, employing my pharmaceutical expertise to the benefit of people's health and well-being.
I fully agree. Unfortunately, the opposite is true when the patient is too stubborn,
and they refuse to listen to us. So true. In other developments, we've had a lot of people coming in
to get their flu shots, which is always good to see. Good. Good. I've been working on a new
medication therapy management program for our patients with chronic conditions. It helps
patients manage their medications more effectively. That sounds interesting. We review all of
of their medications, and make sure that they're taking them as prescribed. We also look for
any potential drug interactions or side effects. Patient response has so far been very positive.
Some have reported seeing improvements in their health, which is really rewarding to see.
That's great to hear. Do you use text message reminders? Yes, absolutely.
It's a great idea. Medication, non-adherence is a big problem, especially for older patients.
We're still in the early stages of the program, but I'm hopeful that it will make a real
difference for our patients. Questions five to eight are based on the conversation you have just heard.

Passage one. In America, at least, passion is a word that often comes up on job descriptions
and in interviews. On the whole, passionate people are thought of in a positive light
and considered likely to achieve their goals. But when it comes to predicting achievement,
has the importance of passion been overstated? According to a new study from Stanford University,
passion may be less important in certain cultures. And the fact that passion is often seen as a
key to achievement may reflect a distinctly western model of motivation. The chief factor explored in
the study was how individualistic a society was. In individualistic cultures, the researchers
assert people are more motivated by pursuing paths related to their passions. But those in
collectivistic cultures are more likely to see themselves as part of a network. They often place
fulfilling obligations to others, above focusing on their own interests. The researchers looked at
data from nearly 60 countries. They found that in science subjects, passion was positively correlated
with academic achievements. Higher levels of enjoyment and interest also bolstered test scores.
But the strength of this correlation wasn't the same across cultures. Those in individualistic
societies, such as the US, Australia, and the UK, showed a stronger link between passion and
achievement. The effective passion and performance was more subtle for those in more collectivistic
societies such as Columbia or Thailand. These findings were mirrored in achievement in both mathematics
and reading. It's clear from the findings that passion isn't the only thing that motivates people
to achieve their goals. Questions 9-11 are based on the passage you have just heard. Question 9.
What are passionate people considered likely to do in America? Question 10. What does a new study
from Stanford show about the importance of passion in predicting achievement? Question 11.
What did the researchers find about the effect of passion on academic achievement for those in
more collectivistic societies? Passage 2. Why does nature create patterns? The reason patterns
often appear in nature is simple. The same basic physical or chemical processes occur in many
patterns, substances, and organisms as they form. Whether in plants and animals or rocks,
foams, and ice crystals, the intricate patterns that happen in nature come down to what's
happening at the level of atoms and molecules. A pattern in nature is any regularly repeated arrangement
of shapes or colours. Some of the most striking examples include the six-sided arrays of rocks
at Giant's Causeway in the United Kingdom, and the colourful stripes and spots on tropical fish.
Patterns like these begin to form at a small scale when materials undergo processes like drying,
freezing, wrinkling, diffusing, and reacting. Those changes then give rise to complex patterns
at a larger scale that people can see. Imagine delicate frozen crystals on a window during winter.
What creates that pattern? When water freezes, its molecules begin clustering together.
Water molecules have a particular bent shape that causes them to stack into clusters as they freeze.
As the cluster grows, many outside factors, including humidity and temperature,
begin to affect its overall shape. If the water is freezing on a window, for example,
random imperfections on the glass surface affect the stacking and create the larger pattern.
But scientists do not always know the purpose of a pattern, or even if there is one.
The molecular processes involved are simple enough that they might generate a pattern by coincidence.

Recording 1. Many people, myself included, have multiple areas of life they would like to improve.
For example, I would like to reach more people with my writing, to lift heavier weights at the gym,
and to start practicing mindfulness more consistently. Those are just a few of the goals I find
desirable, and you probably have a long list yourself. The problem is, even if we are committed
to working hard on our goals, our natural tendency is to return to our old habits at some point.
Making a permanent lifestyle change is really difficult. Recently, I've come across a few
studies that will make these difficult lifestyle changes a bit easier. As you'll see however,
the approach to mastering many areas of life is somewhat counterintuitive. Research has shown
that you are two to three times more likely to stick with your habits if you make a specific plan
for when, where and how you will perform the behavior. For example, in one study, scientists
ask people to fill out a sentence to specify during the next week they would do at least 20 minutes
of vigorous exercise on which day at what time of day and at or in what place. Research has found
that people who filled out this sentence were two to three times more likely to actually exercise
compared to a control group who did not make plans for their future behavior. Psychologists call
these specific plans implementation intentions because they state when, where and how you
intend to implement a particular behavior. However, follow-up research has discovered
implementation intentions only work when you focus on one thing at a time. In fact,
researchers found that people who try to accomplish multiple goals will less committed
and less likely to succeed than those who focused on a single goal. Another science-based
reason to focus on one thing at a time is that when you begin practicing a new habit,
it requires a lot of conscious effort to remember to do it. After a while, however, the pattern
of behavior becomes easier. Eventually, your new habit becomes a normal routine and the process
is more or less mindless and automatic. The most important thing to note is that there is some
tipping point at which new habits become more or less automatic. The time it takes to build a habit
depends on many factors including how difficult the habit is, your genetics, and more.

Recording 2, it was a lazy, hazy, crazy day on the North Planet Pluto when new horizons
a spacecraft from Earth flew by at a speed of 31,000 miles per hour two years ago.
The spacecraft took a bunch of photos, made some quick measurements of Pluto's atmosphere,
and sent them all back here, giving planetary scientists their first up-close look of the distant
dwarf planet. One of the more bizarre things they found was that the haze in Pluto's atmosphere
was much thicker than previously thought. The planet also had an atmosphere much cooler than
earlier estimates, topping out at minus 333.4 degrees Fahrenheit. Now, a study published in
Nature links those two atmospheric observations. A computer model developed by planetary scientist
she is young and colleagues shows the haze of tiny droplets in the upper atmosphere is likely
scattering light from the sun preventing heat from reaching the planet below. We see hazy skies on
Earth too from time to time whenever solid particles get suspended in the air from water-based
fog to ash from fires to the toxic droplets that make up a thick smog. But on Earth,
the overall temperature of the planet is dominated by the distribution of gases in our atmosphere.
On Pluto, the authors suggest, haze might be more influential. Particles can reflect light from
the sun here on Earth. It happens after volcanoes erupt, emitting clouds of particles that reflect
the sun's rays into the atmosphere. Some people even propose imitating this phenomenon
to alleviate the effects of climate change. But our planet isn't dominated by that process,
or at least it hasn't been for a few billion years. If Pluto's atmosphere is very different
from ours and from that of other nearby planets, it could help scientists expand their understanding
of planetary atmospheres. But right now, this is just a good guess based on data from new horizons
and a sophisticated computer model, not direct observations of the hazy's composition.
There are other theories floating around to explain Pluto's cool temperatures,
including blaming the cold air on gases in the atmosphere. Luckily, the authors will get a chance
to test their notions when the James Webb Space Telescope launches later. That observatory
can detect different spectrums of light, which the hazy plutonium atmosphere would be positively
glowing with as it scattered sunlight. The researchers just have to wait and see if the light
from the telescope validates their bright idea. Questions 19 to 21 are based on the recording you
have just heard. Question 19. What was one of the more bizarre findings about Pluto's atmosphere?
Question 20. What is said to determine the overall temperature on Earth? Question 21. What does the
speaker say the researchers have to wait and see? Recording 3. Parents have a small window where
they can influence their 8 to 10-year-old children's music taste researchers have concluded.
The 24-month timeframe comes at an age when youngsters are old enough to appreciate poetic lyrics
and snappy tunes, but have not yet started to be embarrassed by their mother and father's preferences.
Dr. Hawke Eggman, a lecturer in music at the University of York, carried out a literature review
into more than a dozen studies looking at parental musical influence. Children have an openness to
new music and this means parents have an important role to play in developing the musical preferences
of their kids he said. However, time is of the essence as parental influence is most likely to be
effective during the critical time period before age 10. During adolescence children tend to gravitate
away from their parents' choices and are more influenced by their peers. A separate survey of 2000
British parents by music streaming service, these are also found that nearly four fifths of parents
agreed that their children were far more receptive to their musical suggestions before the age of 10.
In contrast, just 10% of parents reported positive reactions from their teenage children when they
shared their favorite music. Some 79% of fathers said they had tried to influence their children's
music but just 69% of mothers. However, mothers were more effective with 38% reporting that their kids
loved the tunes they shared. Compared to 30% of dads who in some cases said their children cried or
even fell asleep. Dr. Eggman claims introducing children to a variety of musical styles is the
key to fostering good taste in later life. By playing children of a variety of genres before this
period, research on familiarization suggests they will enjoy lots of different types of music as adults
he added. The benefits of having a wider taste in music include the ability to manage their emotions
more effectively, socialise and bond with others more easily and to have a better understanding of
other cultures as well. Dr. Eggman advises parents not to push their favorite music too hard on their
but instead play it as background music while a child is playing. They can also help create positive
memories about artists and bands by going to concerts and live music events together.
